questions.q: What is the problem in this code?
questions.hint: What happens if NTP turns the clock between the two readings?

options.text: DateTimeImmutable is slow; you should use DateTime instead
options.why: Speed isn't the issue. Both classes read the same wall clock, so the problem stays.

options.text: It subtracts two wall-clock readings; if the clock is corrected in between, the result is wrong or negative. You need hrtime(true)
options.why: Measuring how long something took is a job for a monotonic clock. hrtime(true) never goes backwards.

options.text: getTimestamp() gives only whole seconds; using microtime(true) would fix it
options.why: microtime() does give a finer reading, but it is still the wall clock. The jump problem remains exactly as before.

options.text: Nothing is wrong; with NTP on, the clock is always right
options.why: NTP is what makes the clock jump. Correcting a clock means its reading changes suddenly.

questions.q: A report shows an order canceled 30 ms before it was created. The create and the cancel happened on two different servers. What is the most likely cause?
questions.hint: Do the wall clocks of two classrooms show exactly the same time?

options.text: The customer really did cancel before ordering
options.why: You can't cancel an order that doesn't exist yet. The real order of events was fine; only the timestamps are wrong.

options.text: The two servers' clocks have skew, so the timestamps came out in the wrong order
options.why: If the server that created the order has a clock running ahead, the later cancel gets a smaller timestamp.

options.text: The two servers are set to different time zones
options.why: A time zone mistake would give a difference of whole or half hours, not 30 milliseconds.

options.text: The database wrote the rows in the reverse order
options.why: The order rows were written in doesn't change a timestamp's value. Each server stamped its own clock's time.

questions.q: In which of these jobs should you use the monotonic clock (hrtime)?
questions.hint: Which ask "how long", and which ask "when"?

options.text: Measuring how many milliseconds an API call took
options.why: This is a "how long" question, a job for the stopwatch.

options.text: Filling an order's created_at column
options.why: This is a "when" question. An hrtime() value is not a date; you need the wall clock's UTC time.

options.text: Running a polling loop for at most 5 seconds
options.why: With a wall clock, a clock jump could make the loop run for ages or stop immediately.

options.text: Printing the date on an invoice
options.why: A date shown to people comes from the wall clock.

options.text: Checking whether 2 seconds have passed since the last retry
options.why: You are measuring the gap between two moments, so use the monotonic clock.

questions.q: A subscription expires after 30 days, and Rachel wants to test that. What is the best way?
questions.hint: Who decides what "now" is inside the test?

options.text: Wait with sleep() in the test
options.why: Waiting 30 days is impossible. Even for short expiries, sleep makes tests slow and unreliable.

options.text: Manually put an old date into expires_at in the database
options.why: That doesn't test the code that calculates the expiry, and "now" is still outside your control.

options.text: Inject ClockInterface and use MockClock in the test to move time forward 30 days
options.why: Once you own the clock, you can check both sides of the boundary, just before and just after, in an instant.

options.text: Change the server's clock before running the tests
options.why: That upsets everything else on the machine, and on a CI server you often can't do it at all.

questions.q: NTP is on for every server. Can you assume two servers' clocks are exactly the same?
questions.hint: The custodian sets the clocks once a day. What do they do in between?

options.text: Yes. Making all the clocks the same is NTP's whole job
options.why: NTP reduces the difference; it doesn't remove it. Network delay and drift always leave some.

options.text: No. NTP reduces skew but doesn't make it zero, and when correcting it can make the clock jump
options.why: In good conditions the difference is a few milliseconds. So the order of events close together in time can't be told by timestamps.

options.text: Yes, if the two servers are in the same data center
options.why: Being in one place makes the difference smaller, but not zero. Each machine's crystal runs at its own pace.

options.text: No, so it's better to turn NTP off
options.why: Without NTP, drift builds up and the difference grows from seconds to minutes. You need NTP; you just shouldn't trust it blindly.

questions.q: A mobile app sends the phone's time (clientTime) with every request. Which of these uses are safe?
questions.hint: Who sets the phone's clock, and can they change it?

options.text: Keeping it in the logs for debugging
options.why: It does no harm as information, and it even shows how wrong phone clocks are.

options.text: Using it to decide whether a coupon has expired
options.why: A user can set their phone's date back and use an expired coupon. The server's clock decides expiry.

options.text: Using it to decide which of two edits came later
options.why: Two phones' clocks can differ by minutes. Whoever's clock is ahead wins, even with an older edit.

options.text: Comparing it with the server's time to measure how wrong the phone's clock is
options.why: Here you aren't trusting the phone's time; you are checking it.

questions.q: A loop is written like this: `$deadline = time() + 5; while (time() < $deadline) { ... }`. While it runs, NTP sets the server's clock back 1 hour. What happens?
questions.hint: If the clock reading suddenly gets smaller, how long until it reaches $deadline?

options.text: The loop stops immediately
options.why: It would stop immediately if the clock jumped forward. Going back moves time() further away from $deadline.

options.text: Nothing changes; PHP uses its own internal clock
options.why: time() reads the system wall clock every time. PHP has no separate clock.

options.text: The loop keeps running for about 1 hour
options.why: time() dropped by an hour, so it takes over an hour to reach $deadline again. Written with hrtime(), this wouldn't happen.

options.text: PHP throws an exception
options.why: To PHP, a clock change is not an error; it doesn't even notice. That is why this kind of bug strikes silently.

questions.q: What is the problem in this code?
questions.hint: Who creates updatedAt, and from whose clock?

options.text: Two machines have different clocks, so a newer change can be lost
options.why: Comparing timestamps doesn't give cause-and-effect order; the stale write from the clock that runs ahead wins.

options.text: replaceWith() is very slow
options.why: Speed isn't the issue here. Correctness is.

options.text: It should be `>=` instead of `>`
options.why: Changing the operator doesn't fix the underlying problem, the wrong clock.

options.text: There is no problem; the clocks are synced with NTP
options.why: NTP still leaves differences of milliseconds to seconds, and the client's clock is outside your control.

questions.q: Server A's counter is 4 and it sends a message. Server B's counter is 9. What is B's new counter when it receives the message?
questions.hint: max(own, received) + 1.

options.why: That is the number after A's counter. B can't ignore its own 9.
max(9, 4) + 1 = 10. A counter never goes backwards.
Adding the two counters is not the rule. The rule is the larger one + 1.
Receiving a message is an event too, so the counter goes up by at least 1.

questions.q: Which statements about a Lamport clock are true?
questions.hint: Think about the difference between cause-and-effect and concurrent.

options.text: If X causes Y, then counter(X) < counter(Y)
options.why: The counter travels with messages, so the receiver always gets a larger number.

options.text: A smaller counter always means the event happened earlier
options.why: For concurrent events the counters can go either way. That doesn't mean earlier or later.

options.text: Ties on equal counters can be broken with the node id to make a total order
options.why: The (counter, node id) pair gives everyone the same total order, though the order among concurrent events is arbitrary.

options.text: It stores the real clock time
options.why: It is only a counter and says nothing about time.

questions.q: Version 7 is already stored. Now a late event for version 6 arrives. What does the handler below do?
questions.code:
UPDATE customer_view SET name = :name, version = :v
WHERE id = :id AND version < :v;
questions.hint: Does the WHERE condition match?

options.text: The condition doesn't match and 0 rows change; the stale event can safely be dropped
options.why: The row has version 7, and 7 < 6 is false. The state stays correct.

options.text: It writes version 6 and puts the row back to its old state
options.why: That is exactly what the condition prevents. A smaller version is never written.

options.text: It throws an exception and the message is retried
options.why: An UPDATE that matches no rows is not an error; it just returns 0.

questions.q: A multi-region database needs near-clock time and also has to preserve cause-and-effect order. Which approach fits?
questions.hint: Time plus a small counter.

options.text: Wall-clock timestamps alone
options.why: Clock errors break the order.

options.text: A hybrid logical clock
options.why: The (clock time, counter) pair gives the benefits of both.

options.text: A separate running number on each server
options.why: Numbers from different servers can't be compared, so there is no global order.

options.text: The time sent by the client
options.why: The client's clock is outside your control and untrustworthy.

questions.q: In which cases is it acceptable to live with last-write-wins?
questions.hint: How much do you lose if a write is lost?

options.text: A "last seen" field
options.why: Even if it is wrong, nothing is lost; it corrects itself next time.

options.text: A temporary value held in a cache
options.why: A wrong value expires with its TTL and comes back from the source.

options.text: A user's saved address
options.why: If the address is lost, deliveries go to the wrong place. You need to detect the conflict.

options.text: The content of a shared document
options.why: Silently erasing someone's work is direct harm. Here you need a merge or conflict handling.

questions.q: Phone A saved version 4. Phone B loaded version 3 earlier and now saves, sending "expected version 3". What happens with version-based locking?
questions.hint: Does the server compare clocks or versions?

options.text: The server answers 409; B fetches version 4 and merges, or asks the user
options.why: The version B saw (3) no longer matches the row (4), so the conflict is caught and nothing is lost silently.

options.text: B silently overwrites A's change
options.why: That is last-write-wins. The version check exists to stop exactly this.

options.text: Whichever phone has the later clock time wins
options.why: No clock is involved in a version check, which is its whole point.

questions.q: An app sends a user in New York a report "every Sunday at 9 pm". The user moves to London and changes zone. Which design is right?
questions.hint: What does the user want: one UTC moment, or 9 o'clock on their own clock?

options.text: Store the user's local 9 pm and their zone name; compute the UTC each time
options.why: The user wants 9 by their own clock. When the zone changes you only change the name, and the calculation fixes itself.

options.text: Store the UTC hour computed once (say 02:00 UTC) forever
options.why: When DST changes, or the zone does, that time slides on the user's clock.

options.text: 9 pm in the server's zone
options.why: Where the server is means nothing to the user.

options.text: Store the offset "-05:00"
options.why: The offset is wrong once the user goes to London, or across a DST change.

questions.q: Which of these should be stored in UTC (timestamptz)?
questions.hint: Which are moments that happened once?

options.text: The time a payment succeeded
options.why: A fixed moment; it stays unchanged in UTC.

options.text: The time a user logged in
options.why: A past event; you change the zone only when displaying it.

options.text: The original time of next Monday's 10 am meeting in London
options.why: This is a future local event. Local time plus the zone name should be the primary data.

options.text: A schedule like "the shop opens at 8 am every day"
options.why: It is a wall-clock rule, not a fixed moment.

questions.q: What will `$next` hold in this code?
questions.hint: DST begins in London on March 29, 2026. Which zone does modify work in?

options.text: 2026-04-06 10:00 BST: the same wall clock, and 09:00 in UTC
options.why: modify() works in that object's zone, so local 10:00 stays intact and the UTC time shifts by an hour.
Adding 168×2 hours would give that, but modify('+2 weeks') counts days.

options.text: An exception
options.why: Crossing a DST change raises no exception.

questions.q: A job is scheduled for 01:30 local time in London on March 29, 2026. What happens?
questions.hint: Where does the clock jump to from 01:00 that day?

options.text: That time doesn't exist (a gap); PHP quietly moves it to 02:30 BST
options.why: A local time inside the spring DST gap is invalid. Moving it silently is dangerous, so set your own rule.

options.text: The job runs at exactly 01:30
options.why: That local time never appears on the clock.

options.text: The job runs twice
options.why: Appearing twice happens in the autumn overlap, not in spring.

options.text: PHP throws an exception
options.why: PHP's DateTimeImmutable raises no error here; it just shifts the time.

questions.q: A user books 01:30 on October 25, 2026 in Europe/London. What should your code do?
questions.hint: How many real moments read 01:30 on that clock?

options.text: List both moments (00:30Z and 01:30Z), pick earlier or later on purpose, and store the UTC
options.why: The wall time matches two instants. Choosing one deliberately, and storing it in UTC, removes the guesswork.

options.text: Pass it to DateTimeImmutable and store whatever comes back
options.why: PHP silently picks one of the two, and the pick can differ between PHP versions.

options.text: Refuse it, because the time does not exist
options.why: That is the spring gap. In autumn the time exists twice.

questions.q: Which of these are good practices?
questions.hint: Think about ways to reduce ambiguity.

options.text: Sending times from the API as ISO 8601 UTC (ending in Z)
options.why: It means the same moment to everyone, and the client shows it in its own zone.

options.text: Storing the zone name, not an offset, for future events
options.why: The name lets you work out the right offset for each date.

options.text: Setting the server's timezone to match the user's timezone
options.why: Users are in thousands of zones. Servers normally stay on UTC.

options.text: Sending the time string "2026-04-06 09:00" without a zone
options.why: The client will assume local time and get it wrong.

questions.q: In the browser of a user in America/New_York, what will `new Date('2026-04-06T09:00:00Z')` correspond to, as the correct local time?
questions.hint: New York is on daylight time in April, which is UTC-4.

options.text: 05:00 (5 am) in New York
options.why: 09:00 UTC - 4 hours = 05:00 in New York, because daylight time began on March 8. This is what Intl does.

options.text: 09:00 in the morning
options.why: That is UTC, not the user's local time.
That uses the winter offset (UTC-5). In April New York is on daylight time, UTC-4.

questions.q: A trial lasts 30 days. Which of these designs is the safest?
questions.hint: Whose clock is easiest to change?

options.text: Count 30 days from the phone's date
options.why: A user can set the date back and run the trial forever.

options.text: Store `trial_ends_at` on the server and compare it with the server's Clock on each request
options.why: The decision is in the server's hands, and the deadline is stored. The client can change nothing.

options.text: Run a stopwatch on the phone from the first launch
options.why: The stopwatch is lost if the app closes or the phone reboots, and everything on the client can be changed.

options.text: Store nothing and ask the user each time
options.why: Whatever the user says, the server can't verify it.

questions.q: Which are the right ways to show a countdown?
questions.hint: Will the countdown stay right if the phone's date is wrong?

options.text: The server sends "300 seconds left" and the client counts down with `performance.now()`
options.why: The phone's date is out of it. A monotonic timer runs at its own pace.

options.text: The server sends expires_at and the client works out the remainder with `Date.now()`
options.why: If the phone's clock is wrong, the countdown is wrong.

options.text: Even when the countdown ends, the final check is on the server
options.why: A countdown is only UX. The real decision is the server's.

options.text: When the countdown hits 0, the client discards the code and doesn't send it to the server
options.why: If the server has a small grace and the client runs slow, a valid code gets thrown away.

questions.q: What is the problem in this code?
questions.hint: Which clock does microtime() read, and what if NTP changes the clock in between?

options.text: It is the wall clock; if NTP changes the clock, the duration can come out wrong. hrtime(true) is safe
options.why: Measuring a duration needs a monotonic clock. If the clock goes backwards you also get negative or jumpy times.

options.text: The if condition is the wrong way round
options.why: The condition is fine. The problem is the clock used to measure.

options.text: microtime() isn't accurate to the second
options.why: The precision is enough. The problem is clock jumps.

questions.q: In an order request the client waits 3 seconds. The inner gateway call has `max_duration` of 1 second, 2 retries, and delays of 0.2 + 0.4 seconds. What is the worst-case total, and is it OK?
questions.hint: 3 attempts + the delays.

options.text: 3 seconds, which is fine
options.why: It leaves out the delays.

options.text: 3.6 seconds, over the limit; the per-attempt limit has to come down
options.why: 3 × 1 + 0.2 + 0.4 = 3.6 > 3. The client gives up first.

options.text: 1 second, because the retries run at the same time
options.why: Retries run one after another, not at the same time.

options.text: Unlimited, because there are retries
options.why: max_retries is bounded, so the total is bounded.

questions.q: Which of these are true about `max_duration`?
questions.hint: HttpClient's total limit, and what 0 means.

options.text: It is the maximum total time for the whole request + response
options.why: It even catches a server that sends data very slowly.

options.text: A value of 0 makes it time out immediately
options.why: 0 or less means unlimited, so when the budget is spent you must check that first.

options.text: It is a synonym for the idle timeout
options.why: The idle timeout is a different option (`timeout`). This one counts total time.

options.text: It applies separately to each retry attempt
options.why: Each attempt gets its own limit, so the total time of the retries has to be worked out separately.

questions.q: A gateway call timed out. Which view is right?
questions.hint: Does no reply mean the work wasn't done?

options.text: The work failed, so it is safe to charge again
options.why: The money may already be taken, with only the reply missing. A second charge would take it twice.

options.text: The outcome is unknown; retry with the same idempotency key, or ask for the status
options.why: A timeout means "I got no reply", not "I know the result". The safe path is the same key or a status query.

options.text: It succeeded, so assume that
options.why: That is a guess too. If it is wrong, the goods go out and the money never arrives.
